name: Lambda AI cloud GPU instances (NVIDIA H100 SXM, self-serve)
region: US-based (Lambda does not itemise regions on the pricing page)
price_basis: per GPU-hour, 8-GPU instance (208 vCPU / 1800 GiB / 22 TiB SSD): H100 SXM $3.99; A100 SXM 80GB $2.79; A100 SXM 40GB $1.99; B200 SXM6 $6.69; V100 $0.79. Smaller shapes are dearer per GPU: 4x H100 $4.09, 2x H100 $4.19, 1x H100 SXM $4.29, 1x H100 PCIe $3.29, 1x GH200 96GB $2.29. Quote is '+ applicable sales tax/VAT/GST'. Fetched 2026-10-03. PRICE CLASS: this is a PUBLISHED LIST PRICE - an asking rate a new customer is quoted, not a realised, discounted or negotiated transaction rate. A real bill is at or below this and typically well below it once commitments, credits and committed-use discounts are applied.
notes:
THE CHEAPEST CREDIBLE ON-DEMAND H100 HOUR ON A DEDICATED 8-GPU NODE IN THIS SLICE: $3.99/GPU-hour against $6.88 on AWS p5 and $11.06 on Google a3 - about 42% under AWS and 64% under GCP. Self-serve, first-come, no sales call, which also makes it the best-evidenced record here after the hyperscaler APIs. A counter-intuitive and useful detail: on Lambda the per-GPU price FALLS with node size ($4.29 single, $4.19 dual, $4.09 quad, $3.99 octuple), so take the 8-GPU node - the opposite of GCP G2, where the small node is cheaper. If you only need one H100, the PCIe single at $3.29 is the cheapest single H100 in the slice. Two caveats. (1) The 1-Click Cluster tiers are a DIFFERENT and more expensive product: H100 at $6.16/GPU-hr for 16 GPUs, $5.85 at 64, $5.54 at 256, all quote-only via a sales call - so 'Lambda H100' is ambiguous between $3.99 self-serve and $6.16 clustered, and the clustered number is worse than AWS p5 on-demand. Quote the Instances price, not the Clusters price, unless you need the colocation. (2) lambdalabs.com/service/gpu-cloud/pricing is a 404 - the live page is lambda.ai - so old links and blog posts citing the old domain are stale. No published commitment discount: reserved capacity is a sales conversation.

 EXPORT CONTROL (2026-10-04, mechanism-level; sources spl-bis-2026-05-d5-guidance, spl-bis-2026-01-advanced-computing-case-by-case): renting capacity does NOT remove the export-control question, it relocates it. Providing remote access to controlled computing capability can constitute a transfer under the EAR, so the provider must screen the end user; and separately, under the 91 FR 1684 licence regime the consignee must run KYC procedures to prevent unauthorized remote access and must manage and limit IaaS access to the hardware - obligations pushed onto the customer, who must be told to implement them. For a customer headquartered or parented in Country Group D:5 or Macau the 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) end-user/parent test can bite even when the capacity is consumed in a permitted region. Recorded true because the underlying hardware is controlled and the provider carries the screening duty, not because access to a US region is itself restricted.

 LEAD TIME: null, and correct as null. For a listed on-demand instance type the provisioning delay is effectively zero - capacity is allocated per request - so a week count would be meaningless; the real gate for scarce shapes is either a quota increase or a capacity reservation, not a lead time. Where a published commitment horizon exists it IS recorded: AWS documents that a Capacity Block may be reserved with a start time up to EIGHT WEEKS in the future (source spl-aws-capacity-block-booking-horizon), which is a floor on how far ahead scarce capacity must be committed, not a wait. On-demand and Spot tiers publish no lead time at all; their constraint is availability, and the repo records that as availability=in-stock or a spot/reality note rather than as a fabricated week figure. Probe log in source spl-negative-no-oem-publishes-lead-time.
